items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: Now, they say that this, but Freddie Kepit, they make a great big story about it, that he was asked by the Victor Company to record.

ctx.x: No, I wrote that mostly as a sort of, you might say, editor. Walter Allen managed to interview the various musicians that were still living. And he sent me the facts and I wrote them, sewed them up together. I was more concerned with the records than with the legends. I wasn't very interested in these obscure people from the shadows who were said to have played with this, that and the other musician, in this, that and the other band, and who never made any records at all. I'm not interested in music I can't hear…

Now, they say that this, but Freddie Kepit, they make a great big story about it, that he was asked by the Victor Company to record. He says he didn't want to record because he didn't want the world to know his stuff. But they didn't know that I knew all this stuff. They thought that I was just a dumb man, that I didn't know what was going on. They imported them all. The Kepits, the Olivers, and all of them, they all died in the gutter. None of them made good. None of them could make a record. They had to steal…

So that the opening words of the late Jelly Roll Morton on his talk for the Library of Congress in Washington, with Alan Lomax, is wrong completely. He says from the very first, the first words he says on those records is, jazz started in New Orleans. And he goes on to tell about how he wrote Tiger Rag, how he named it, and how it was based on the old French quadrilles and all the rest of that stuff. Well, you've told me already, and I believe you absolutely, that that is just so much hooey.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: Buddy Bolin, Freddie Kepler, George Pequet left here in 1911.

ctx.x: Pioneer of jazz wins recognition, New Orleans, editor from New Orleans States. It was gratifying to read in your paper on February 27th the article on Nick LaRocca, famous leader of the original Dixieland jazz band. He deserves the honor accorded him and his band by the Jazz Club of England whose leader, Marcus O'Donoghau visited our sea last summer. If Mr. LaRocca accepts this invitation, and I hope he does, I'm sure he will mention some of the other bands that played jazz at that time. Tom Brown, who took his…

I'd like to comment on the dates that she has here to show you she was eaten up, taken in by this communist propaganda. I wish you'd hear this tape recorder. Buddy Bolin, Freddie Kepler, George Pequet left here in 1911. In 1906, by the things that I have in my hand, from Louisiana State Mental Hospital at Jackson, Louisiana, Bolin was incarcerated in there in 1906. He couldn't have played with them. And I've told you when these Negroes came it was 1917. Clarence Williams, he says, left here around 1911 or 13.…
In this letter. In this letter. In this letter.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: After this time came King Oliver, Punk, and Freddie Capron, that's spelled K-E-P-P-E-R-T, and the original Creole Band.

ctx.x: It is an original Negro tune, which was made up down south. It was named Tiger Rag when the Dixieland Band brought it up north. Buddy, you want me to continue with this? Yeah, go on. Buddy Bolden was the hottest cornetist in the world, and he played so much that he is in the insane asylum now if he is still living. After this time came King Oliver, Punk, and Freddie Capron, that's spelled K-E-P-P-E-R-T, and the original Creole Band. They were the last word and swing cornet players. The swing pianists were Albert…

We used to have swing sessions every morning around 3 o'clock after the boys got through with their work and each man would do his bit. Quote, the first hot band to leave from the South and introduce swing music was the Creole Jazz Band, unquote, says Mr. Williams. Quote, following the Dixieland Jazz Band, which recorded Livery Stable Blues and Tiger Ray, which swept the country. The Creole Band was colored and the Dixieland Band was white and they used to play across the street from each other and used to sit in…
